subject: rla
title: Word Meaning, Tone, and Figurative Language
objectives: You will use context clues (definition, example, contrast, and cause and effect) and the replacement test to find what a word means as it is used in a text.
You will tell a word's denotation from its connotation and explain how an author's word choice creates a positive, negative, or neutral feeling.
You will name the tone (the writer's or narrator's attitude) and the mood (the reader's feeling) of a passage, find where they shift, and prove each with words from the text.
You will identify similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, and idioms and explain what each one suggests and why the author used it.
You will answer GED-style word meaning, tone, and figurative language questions, including drop-down word-choice items and click-the-sentence items.

slides.title: Word Meaning, Tone, and Figurative Language
slides.board:
Week 4 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Use context clues to find what a word means here
  • Tell denotation from connotation
  • Name the tone and the mood, and prove them
  • Read similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, and idioms
  • Answer GED-style word and language questions

Plan: Warm-up · Word meaning · Feeling words · Tone and mood · Figurative language · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: This week we move into literary reading: stories and personal narratives. About a quarter of the GED reading passages are literary, and they are full of questions about words: what a word means in this sentence, what feeling it carries, what a comparison suggests, and what attitude the writer takes. Here is the good news I want you to hear first: these questions reward careful readers, not people with giant vocabularies. You do not need to know every word. You need to know how to use the sentence around it.
ask: When someone texts you “Fine.” with a period, how does it feel compared with “Fine!”? (expected: the period sounds cold or annoyed; the exclamation point sounds friendly. Use it to say that small word choices carry feeling, which is today's whole topic.)

slides.title: Warm-up: last week's skills
slides.board:
Answer out loud.

  1. “Because the bridge closed, buses were rerouted, and commutes grew by 20 minutes.” Which structure: chronological, cause and effect, or compare and contrast?
  2. An article opens with a short story about one family losing power for a week, then explains the city's new storm plan. Why open with the story?
  3. Which signal word shows contrast: next, therefore, or unlike?
steps: 1. Cause and effect. Because signals a cause; the reroute and longer commutes are effects.
2. To hook the reader and make the problem feel real before explaining the solution.
3. Unlike. Next shows time order; therefore shows a result.

notes.say: Last week was text structure, author's purpose, and point of view. These three questions check that it stuck, and each one connects to today. Signal words are context clues in disguise, and purpose questions (“why does the author…?”) are exactly the questions we will ask about word choice today. Give about 30 seconds per question.
notes.answer: 1. Cause and effect. 2. To grab attention and show the human cost of the problem (an anecdote hook). 3. Unlike.
notes.watch: If the student says “chronological” for question 1 because events happen in order, ask, “Does the sentence explain why something happened?” Then circle because.

slides.title: Warm-up: point of view and feeling
slides.board:
“I told myself I wasn't nervous. I checked my tie four times in the elevator.”

  1. Is this first person or third person? How do you know?
  2. Do you believe the narrator is not nervous? What detail tells you?
  3. Which word feels warmer: house or home?
steps: 1. First person: the narrator says “I” and “myself.”
2. No. Checking a tie four times shows nerves, so this narrator is not completely reliable.
3. Home feels warmer. House is just the building; home suggests belonging. That difference is today's first big idea.

notes.say: Point of view was the last piece of week 3. A first-person narrator can tell us one thing while the details show another, and noticing that gap is how we will read tone today. Question 3 is a preview: two words with nearly the same meaning can feel very different.
ask: What does the tie detail show that the narrator will not say? (expected: he is nervous)
notes.answer: 1. First person (“I,” “myself”). 2. No; checking the tie four times shows nervousness. 3. Home; it suggests family and belonging, while house is neutral.

slides.title: Context clues: four kinds
slides.board:
ClueLook forExample
Definitiona comma, dash, or semicolon that explainsHe was frugal; he never wasted a dollar.
Examplesuch as, includingcitrus fruits such as lemons and limes
Contrastbut, although, unlikeUnlike her chatty sister, Rosa was reticent.
Cause/effectso, because, as a resultThe road was so treacherous that school closed.

notes.say: When you hit a word you do not know, do not skip it and do not panic. The sentence almost always hands you a clue. Walk through the four kinds. The contrast clue is the most powerful: if Rosa is the opposite of chatty, she must be quiet. The cause-and-effect clue works the same way: a road that closes schools must be dangerous. Your job is to find the clue word, then ask what the unknown word has to mean for the sentence to make sense.
ask: In the Rosa sentence, what does reticent mean, and which word gave it away? (expected: quiet or reserved; unlike plus chatty)
Which clue type is “so treacherous that school closed”? (expected: cause and effect)
notes.watch: Students sometimes take the clue word itself as the meaning (“reticent means chatty”). Stress that a contrast clue gives the opposite.

slides.title: Using a clue: what does it mean?
slides.board:
“Darnell expected the job fair to be sparse, but by ten o'clock the gym was packed, and the line for the hospital's table stretched out the door.”

What does sparse mean here?
steps: Step 1, find the clue: but signals a contrast. What Darnell expected is the opposite of what happened.
Step 2, what happened: the gym was packed and the line stretched out the door.
Step 3, flip it: the opposite of packed is thinly attended, with few people.
Step 4, replacement test: “Darnell expected the job fair to be nearly empty, but … the gym was packed.” It works. Sparse = thin, few in number.

notes.say: Model the thinking out loud. Find the clue word first, decide what kind of clue it is, then build a meaning and test it. Make a point of the last step: we always put our meaning back into the sentence.
ask: What kind of clue was this? (expected: contrast, signaled by but)

slides.title: “As used in the passage” and the replacement test
slides.board:
Many words have several meanings: modest, bright, sharp, cold, run, settle.

Replacement test

  1. Cover the word.
  2. Put each answer choice in its place.
  3. Reread the sentence (and the one before it).
  4. Keep the choice that fits this sentence.

Trap: a real meaning of the word that does not fit here.

notes.say: The GED loves the phrase “as used in paragraph 3.” That phrase is a warning: the answer is often not the first meaning that comes to mind. Test makers put a real dictionary meaning in the choices on purpose, because they know students will recognize it. The replacement test beats that trap every time, because a wrong meaning makes the sentence sound wrong.
ask: Give two meanings of sharp. (expected: any two, such as able to cut, smart, sudden, stylish, exactly on time)
Which meaning fits “She arrived at nine o'clock sharp”? (expected: exactly on time)
notes.watch: Some students stop at the first choice that “sounds like” the word. Require them to say the replacement sentence out loud.

slides.title: A correct meaning in the wrong place
slides.board:
“After the plant closed, Ray took a job at the hardware store. The pay was modest, but the hours were steady, and he liked being home for dinner.”

As used here, modest most nearly means:
A. humble about one's success   B. small or limited
C. shy around others   D. plain in style
steps: Clue: but sets up a contrast. The pay is a drawback; the steady hours are a benefit.
Test A: “The pay was humble about its success.” Pay cannot be humble. Out.
Test C: “The pay was shy.” Shyness describes people. Out.
Test D: “plain in style” fits clothes or houses, not a paycheck. Out.
B: “The pay was small, but the hours were steady.” It fits. Answer: B.

notes.say: Every choice here is a real meaning of modest or close to it. That is what makes this question hard. Show how the contrast clue and the replacement test decide it.
ask: Which wrong choice is the most common meaning of modest? (expected: A, humble)

slides.title: Find the meaning together
slides.board:
“The new manager was candid with the crew. She told them plainly that sales were down, that overtime would be cut, and that she did not yet know whether the store would stay open past June.”

1. What clue type? 2. What does candid mean? 3. Test it.
steps: Clue type: definition / restatement. The second sentence shows what she did: she “told them plainly,” including bad news.
Meaning: honest and direct, even when the truth is unpleasant.
Test: “The new manager was honest and direct with the crew.” It fits.

notes.say: Now the student leads. Ask for the clue first. This one is a definition or restatement clue: the second sentence shows what candid looks like. Reveal each step only after the student answers.
ask: Which word in the second sentence is the strongest clue? (expected: plainly)
Would “cheerful” fit? Why not? (expected: no; the news is bad, and nothing shows cheer)
notes.answer: Restatement clue; candid means honest and direct, open about the truth. Key evidence: “told them plainly,” plus the unpleasant facts she shared.
notes.watch: If the student says “mean” or “harsh,” ask whether anything in the sentence shows she was unkind. Honest is not the same as harsh.

slides.title: Denotation and connotation
slides.board:
Denotation = the dictionary meaning.
Connotation = the feeling the word carries: positive, negative, or neutral.

PositiveNeutralNegative
thriftycareful with moneycheap
curiousinterestednosy
determineddoes not give upstubborn
slimthinscrawny

notes.say: Each row has nearly the same dictionary meaning, but a very different feeling. If I call you thrifty, I am complimenting you. If I call you cheap, I am insulting you. Writers pick words for that feeling on purpose, so a word's connotation is one of the best clues to a writer's attitude. On the GED, any question that asks why the author used a certain word is really a connotation question.
ask: Give a word that means about the same as stubborn but sounds like praise. (expected: determined, persistent, firm)
Is residence positive, negative, or neutral? Compare it with home. (expected: neutral and formal; home is warm)
notes.watch: Students sometimes call a word negative because the situation is sad. Connotation is about the word's own feeling, not the topic.

slides.title: Why did the author choose that word?
slides.board:
Two news stories describe the same city plan to close a road for a farmers market every Saturday.

Story 1: “The mayor's bold plan…”
Story 2: “The mayor's reckless plan…”

What does each word tell you about the writer?
steps: Denotation: both words describe a plan that takes a risk.
Connotation: bold is positive (brave, confident). Reckless is negative (careless about danger).
What it reveals: writer 1 approves of the plan; writer 2 disapproves.
Answer pattern: “The author uses ___ to show that the writer views ___ as ___.”

notes.say: This is the move behind every “why does the author use the word…” question. First state the shared meaning, then the feeling, then what the feeling reveals about the writer.
ask: Give another negative word for the same plan. (expected: risky, foolish, careless)

slides.title: Choose the word that fits the tone
slides.board:
A thank-you note to a retiring school bus driver:

“For twenty-two years, Mr. Okafor has been the most [ ? ] driver on Route 9. Rain or snow, he was at the corner at 7:10.”

A. predictable   B. dependable   C. rigid   D. routine
steps: Purpose: a thank-you note, so the word must be positive.
Rigid is negative: unwilling to bend. Out.
Predictable and routine are neutral or a little dull. Not warm enough for praise. Out.
B. dependable: positive, and the detail (at the corner at 7:10, rain or snow) proves it.

notes.say: This is a GED drop-down move: all four words share part of their meaning (he does the same thing every day), but only one has the right feeling for a thank-you note. Have the student sort the four as positive, neutral, or negative first.
ask: Sort the four words: positive, neutral, or negative. (expected: dependable +; predictable and routine neutral; rigid −)
notes.answer: B. dependable. It is the only clearly positive word, and it matches the evidence that he was always on time in all weather. Rigid is negative; predictable and routine are neutral or slightly dull.
notes.watch: If the student picks predictable, ask, “Would you want this word in your own retirement card?” That usually settles it.

slides.title: Tone: the writer's attitude
slides.board:
Tone = how the writer or narrator feels about the subject.

Ask: How does the writer feel about this?

PositiveNeutralNegative
admiring, affectionate, hopeful, nostalgic, amusedobjective, matter-of-fact, informativebitter, sarcastic, critical, mocking, resentful

Method: highlight strong words → sort + or − → pick the most precise word.

notes.say: Tone is attitude, the way a tone of voice is attitude. The same sentence can be warm or sarcastic depending on the words around it. Teach the three-step method: highlight the strongest words and details, sort them as mostly positive or mostly negative, then choose the most precise tone word. Warn about extreme answers: furious, ecstatic, terrified are almost always wrong unless the text is that extreme.
ask: What is the difference between amused and mocking? (expected: both find something funny; mocking adds scorn or makes fun of someone)
notes.watch: Students often name the topic instead of the tone (“the tone is about work”). A tone answer is always an attitude word.

slides.title: Name the tone and prove it
slides.board:
“Our new manager, Mr. Pratt, loves rules. He has rules about lunch breaks, rules about stacking boxes, and, I am not making this up, a rule about how loudly we may sneeze. Last week he sent a two-page memo about pens.”

Tone? A. admiring   B. amused   C. furious   D. frightened
steps: Highlight: “loves rules,” the repeated “rules about,” “I am not making this up,” “how loudly we may sneeze,” “two-page memo about pens.”
Sort: the details are picked because they sound silly. The narrator is poking fun.
Eliminate: A is the opposite. C is too extreme: nothing shows real anger. D has no support.
Answer: B, amused (a joking, gently mocking attitude).

notes.say: Model the method. Highlight, sort, choose precisely. Then eliminate the extremes out loud so the student hears why they fail.
ask: Which phrase is the strongest clue? (expected: “I am not making this up” or the sneeze rule)

slides.title: Mood, and how it shifts
slides.board:
ToneMood
Whose feeling?the writer's attitudethe reader's feeling
AskHow does the writer feel?How does this make me feel?
Wordsbitter, admiring, amusedtense, gloomy, peaceful, eerie

Shift signals: then, suddenly, but, for the first time, a new paragraph, a change in setting or light.

notes.say: Draw two arrows. One goes from the writer to the subject: that is tone. The other goes from the page to the reader: that is mood. Mood comes from setting, sounds, light, pace, and word choice. Then teach shifts: the GED often asks how the mood changes or which sentence marks the change. Look for a turn word, a new event, or a change in setting, light, or sound.
ask: A calm narrator describes a creaking door at midnight. Can the tone be calm while the mood is tense? (expected: yes; that is the difference between the two)
notes.watch: When a question says “mood,” some students answer with the character's feeling. Ask, “How does the paragraph make you feel?”

slides.title: Track the mood, then find the shift
slides.board: (1) The emergency waiting room was a fishbowl of fluorescent light. (2) Andre had sat in the same plastic chair for three hours, and the clock seemed to drag its hands on purpose. (3) Every time the double doors swung open, his heart leapt into his throat. (4) Then a nurse in green scrubs walked toward him, smiling, and for the first time all night, Andre let out the breath he had been holding.
steps: Sentences 1–3, evidence: three hours in one chair, a clock that “drags its hands,” his heart leaping at every door.
Opening mood: tense and anxious.
The shift: sentence 4. Signals: Then, the smiling nurse, “for the first time all night.”
New mood: relief. The released breath ends the tension.

notes.say: Model it: name the mood of the opening with evidence, then find the sentence where it changes and name the new mood. The word then plus the smile is the hinge.
ask: What does “let out the breath he had been holding” tell us about how he felt before? (expected: he had been tense the whole time)

slides.title: Tone or mood?
slides.board:
“The storm took the porch roof, the shed, and both of Grandpa's tomato cages. He stood in the yard the next morning, hands on his hips, and announced that the tomatoes had always wanted to see the neighbor's garden anyway.”

1. Grandpa's attitude (tone of his remark)? 2. The mood of the scene?
steps: The facts: real damage: porch roof, shed, tomato cages.
Grandpa's tone: good-humored, joking about the loss. Evidence: the tomatoes “always wanted to see the neighbor's garden.”
Mood for the reader: warm and lightly funny, not gloomy, because his joke turns the loss into a smile.

notes.say: The facts are a loss, but the attitude is humor. This passage is a great test of whether the student can separate the subject from the attitude. Ask for evidence every time.
ask: What figure of speech is in Grandpa's joke? (expected: personification; tomatoes cannot want to see a garden)
notes.answer: Tone: good-humored, joking, or resilient (he makes light of the damage). Mood: warm and lightly humorous. Evidence: the personified tomatoes that “always wanted to see the neighbor's garden.” A gloomy answer reads only the facts and ignores the attitude.
notes.watch: If the student says “sad,” point out that the damage is sad but the writer chose to end on a joke. Tone and mood come from how the writer presents the facts.

slides.title: Figurative language: five types
slides.board:
TypeSignalExample
Similelike or asas quiet as a library
Metaphorone thing is anotherThe hallway was a tomb.
Personificationhuman action for a non-human thingThe furnace groaned.
Hyperbolehuge exaggerationI've told you a million times.
Idioma saying whose words don't add upon the fence = undecided

notes.say: Literal language means exactly what it says. Figurative language means more than, or something different from, what it says. Build the table with the student and get an example of each from them. Two warnings: not every like or as makes a simile (“as it cooled” just means “while”), and idioms are fixed sayings everyone uses, while metaphors are fresh comparisons the writer made up.
ask: “The coffee maker sighed as it cooled.” Simile or personification? (expected: personification; as means “while,” and sighing is a human action)
Give an idiom you used this week. (expected: any, such as “hit the road,” “piece of cake”)
notes.watch: Students call every comparison a metaphor. Teach the order: check for like/as making a comparison first, then ask whether one thing is called another.

slides.title: Name it, unpack it, explain the effect
slides.board:
“After my brother left for the Army, hope was a candle my mother kept burning in the front window. Neighbors stopped asking about him after the first year. She never stopped setting his place at the table.”

What does the first sentence suggest about the mother?
steps: Name it: metaphor. “Hope was a candle,” with no like or as.
Unpack it: a candle is small but steady, needs tending to stay lit, and in a window it signals someone to come home.
Effect: her hope is quiet, faithful, and kept alive by effort, a signal for her son's return.
Confirm with context: neighbors stopped asking, but she “never stopped setting his place.”

notes.say: This is the three-step routine for any figure of speech. Do it slowly. The unpacking step is where students earn the point: list what you know about the second thing (a candle in a window), then carry those qualities over to the first thing (her hope).
ask: Why is the candle better than just saying “she hoped he would return”? (expected: it shows how steady and patient her hope was, and it creates an image)

slides.title: Idiom or not? What does it mean?
slides.board:
1. “When the boss asked who broke the copier, Leon spilled the beans.”
  2. “After the double shift, my feet were killing me.”
  3. “Tina is on the fence about taking the night class.”
  4. “The backpack weighed a ton.”
steps: 1. Idiom: revealed the secret (no beans involved).
2. Idiom / hyperbole: my feet hurt a lot.
3. Idiom: undecided.
4. Hyperbole: the backpack was very heavy.

notes.say: Have the student read each literally first and notice that the literal meaning does not fit. Then use the context to decide what it really means. Point out that 2 and 4 are also hyperbole: big exaggerations everyone understands.
ask: How do you know “spilled the beans” is not literal? (expected: the context is about a broken copier; nobody was eating)
notes.answer: 1. Revealed the secret. 2. My feet hurt badly (idiom and hyperbole). 3. Undecided. 4. Very heavy (hyperbole).
notes.watch: Learners who grew up speaking another language may not know an idiom. Teach the backup plan: if the literal meaning makes no sense, use the sentences around it to decide what it must mean.

slides.title: Your turn: word meaning and feeling
slides.board:
3 minutes.

  1. “Unlike her gregarious roommate, who knew everyone on the floor, Maya preferred a quiet night with a book.” Gregarious means ___.
  2. “The air in the basement was stale.” Positive, negative, or neutral?
  3. “The coach's blunt feedback stung, but it was exactly what the team needed.” As used here, blunt means: (a) dull-edged (b) honest and direct (c) rude (d) slow.
steps: 1. Sociable, outgoing. Contrast clue: unlike … Maya preferred a quiet night; the roommate “knew everyone.”
2. Negative. Stale suggests old, unpleasant air. (Compare fresh.)
3. (b) honest and direct. (a) is the knife meaning; (c) is too negative because the feedback was “exactly what the team needed.”

notes.say: Start the timer and stay quiet. The student solves all three, then tells you the answers. Reveal one at a time after they answer, and ask for the clue each time.
notes.answer: 1. Sociable, outgoing (contrast clue). 2. Negative. 3. (b) honest and direct.

slides.title: Your turn: tone and mood
slides.board:
4 minutes.

  1. “The landlord, who could fix nothing, was a genius at sending rent reminders.” Tone: admiring, sarcastic, or neutral?
  2. “Wind rattled the shutters. Somewhere upstairs, a door clicked shut, though no one else was home.” Mood?
  3. “Every summer, we packed into Uncle Ray's station wagon, sticky with orange soda, singing the same three songs. I would give anything for one more of those drives.” Tone?
steps: 1. Sarcastic. “Genius” is praise used to criticize: he cannot fix anything but never forgets rent.
2. Eerie / suspenseful. Rattling wind and a door closing in an empty house.
3. Nostalgic (fond longing for the past). “I would give anything for one more.”

notes.say: Timer on. For each answer, ask the student for the exact words that prove it. A tone or mood answer without evidence does not count on the extended response either.
notes.answer: 1. Sarcastic (or mocking). 2. Eerie, tense, or suspenseful. 3. Nostalgic or fondly wistful.

slides.title: Your turn: figurative language
slides.board:
4 minutes. Name each one and say what it means.

  1. “Her laugh was a siren that cleared the whole room.”
  2. “The old truck coughed twice and died at the light.”
  3. “He runs like a man who left the stove on.”
  4. “Finding a parking spot downtown is like finding a needle in a haystack.”
steps: 1. Metaphor. Her laugh is so loud and startling that it drives people out.
2. Personification. The engine sputtered and stalled, like a sick person.
3. Simile. He runs fast and in a panic.
4. Simile built on an idiom. “A needle in a haystack” means nearly impossible to find.

notes.say: Timer on. The student names the type and explains the meaning. Push for the effect on item 1: a siren is loud, alarming, and makes people move.
notes.answer: 1. Metaphor: loud, alarming laugh. 2. Personification: the truck stalls and sputters. 3. Simile: running fast and frantically. 4. Simile using the idiom “a needle in a haystack”: very hard to find a spot.
notes.watch: On item 4, accept “simile” or “idiom” if the student explains it; the strongest answer names both.

slides.title: GED-style question: word in context
slides.board:
“Mrs. Bell had run the corner store for forty years. Kids who could not pay for a soda left with one anyway, and she settled more neighborhood arguments over that counter than any judge in town.”

As used in the passage, settled most nearly means:

A. moved into a new home
B. resolved or ended
C. paid off a debt
D. sank to the bottom
steps: Predict: she did something to arguments, compared with a judge. She ended them.
A is wrong: “settled into a home” is a real meaning, but you cannot move into an argument.
C is wrong: “settled a bill” is about money. The sentence is about arguments, and the soda detail is a different point.
D is wrong: dust settles; arguments do not sink.
B is right: “resolved more neighborhood arguments than any judge.” The judge comparison confirms it.

notes.say: Do this one the way the student will on test day: read the sentence, predict a meaning before looking at the choices, then eliminate. Each wrong choice is a real meaning of settled.
ask: Which wrong choice did the soda sentence try to pull you toward? (expected: C, paying a debt)
notes.answer: B. A, C, and D are real meanings of settled that do not fit arguments. The comparison with a judge confirms “resolved.”

slides.title: GED-style question: the effect of a comparison
slides.board:
“By the end of her first week on the loading dock, Dani's alarm clock had become a drill sergeant: it barked at 4:30, it did not care how she felt, and it never once let her sleep in.”

What does the metaphor suggest?

A. Dani is thinking about joining the military.
B. The alarm is loud, demanding, and impossible to ignore.
C. Dani's supervisor on the loading dock is strict and rude.
D. The alarm clock is old and often breaks.
steps: A is wrong: it reads “drill sergeant” literally. Nothing mentions the military.
C is wrong: the comparison is about the alarm clock, not her supervisor. It applies the metaphor to the wrong subject.
D is wrong: the text says it “never once” failed to wake her; it works too well, not too poorly.
B is right: a drill sergeant is loud, strict, and unmoved by excuses; the alarm “barked,” “did not care,” and never let her sleep in.

notes.say: Use name, unpack, effect. Then eliminate. Two choices read the metaphor literally, and one moves it onto the wrong thing.
ask: What qualities of a drill sergeant does the writer carry over? (expected: loud, strict, does not care about your feelings)
notes.answer: B. The metaphor gives the alarm a drill sergeant's loud, demanding, unsympathetic qualities; the details “barked,” “did not care,” and “never once let her sleep in” confirm it.

slides.title: GED-style question: tone in a draft
slides.board:
A community center is writing a respectful notice about a beloved volunteer who passed away.

“Mr. Hollis [ ? ] on March 2 at the age of 91. For thirty years, he taught free chess lessons every Saturday.”

A. kicked the bucket   B. passed away
C. was finally gone   D. checked out
steps: Purpose: a respectful notice. The words must be gentle and formal.
A is wrong: “kicked the bucket” is a joking idiom; it disrespects the family.
D is wrong: “checked out” is slang and too casual.
C is wrong: “finally” suggests people were waiting for it, a cold, negative connotation.
B is right: “passed away” is the gentle, respectful standard.

notes.say: This is the GED drop-down format: every choice means about the same thing, and the test is whether the tone fits the purpose. Ask the student to name the purpose and audience before choosing.
ask: Which word in choice C turns it negative? (expected: finally)
notes.answer: B. passed away. It matches the respectful purpose. A and D are slang idioms; C's “finally” adds a cold, negative connotation.

slides.title: GED strategy: put it back and prove it
slides.board:
1. Go to the line. Reread the sentence, plus one before and one after.
  2. Predict the meaning or feeling in your own words.
  3. Put it back: replace the word with each choice and reread.
  4. Prove it: for tone and mood, point to two words that support your answer.
  5. Cut extremes and literal readings.

About 1 minute per word question. Do not reread the whole story.

notes.say: Word questions are the fastest points on the RLA test if you have a routine. Go straight to the line the question names, predict, and put each choice back in the sentence. For tone and mood, require proof: if you cannot point to two words that support your answer, it is probably wrong. And remember the two favorite traps: the extreme feeling word and the literal reading of a figure of speech.
ask: What two traps do test writers use most on these questions? (expected: a real meaning that does not fit the context, and extreme or literal answers)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Context clues + the replacement test find the meaning here.
  • Denotation = dictionary; connotation = feeling.
  • Tone = writer's attitude; mood = reader's feeling. Prove both with words.
  • Figures of speech: name it, unpack it, explain the effect.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Ask the student to give the difference between tone and mood and the three steps for a figure of speech from memory before you reveal the board. Then set up the week: the Student Lesson walks through every skill again with check questions, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check shows whether they are ready for week 5, where we analyze arguments.
ask: What will you do the next time a question says “as used in paragraph 2”? (expected: find the clue, predict, and put each choice back in the sentence)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will read stories and personal narratives, and many questions will ask about the words the writer chose. What does this word mean here? Why did the author pick it? What feeling does this paragraph create? What does this comparison suggest? You do not need a huge vocabulary to answer them. You need a few reliable methods. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • use context clues to find what a word means in this sentence
  • tell a word's denotation (dictionary meaning) from its connotation (the feeling it carries)
  • name the tone (the writer's attitude) and the mood (the reader's feeling), and prove each with words from the text
  • read similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, and idioms and explain what they suggest

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question. If you miss one, read why your answer was wrong before you move on.

screens.title: Context clues: definition and example
screens.html:
A context clue is a hint in the words around an unfamiliar word. Two kinds of clues explain the word for you:

  • Definition or restatement. The sentence explains the word, often after a comma, dash, colon, or semicolon. “Marcus was frugal; he never spent a dollar he did not need to.” The part after the semicolon tells you frugal means careful with money.
  • Example. The sentence gives examples, often after such as, including, or for example. “She loved citrus fruits such as lemons, limes, and oranges.” The examples tell you what citrus fruits are.

When you see one of these clues, read it carefully. The writer is practically handing you the definition.

example.prompt: “The old factory was full of hazards: loose floorboards, exposed wires, and broken glass everywhere.” What does hazards mean?
steps: The colon signals that examples are coming.
The examples (loose floorboards, exposed wires, broken glass) are all things that could hurt you.
Replacement test: “The old factory was full of dangers.” It fits.

check.prompt:
“Root vegetables, such as carrots, beets, and turnips, keep well through the winter.”

Type the two-word phrase in this sentence that signals an example clue.
check.hint: Find the words that come right before the list.
check.explain: The phrase such as introduces the examples: carrots, beets, and turnips. Those examples tell you what root vegetables are: vegetables that grow underground. Such as, including, and for example are the most common example signals.

mistakes.why: That is the term being explained, not the signal. Look for the two words that introduce the list of examples.
That phrase tells what the vegetables do, not how the examples are introduced. Find the words right before “carrots.”

screens.title: Context clues: contrast and cause and effect
screens.html:
Two more kinds of clues make you reason your way to the meaning:

  • Contrast. Words like but, although, however, unlike, and instead tell you the unknown word means the opposite of something nearby. “Unlike his chatty brother, Leo was reticent.” Leo is the opposite of chatty, so reticent means quiet or reserved.
  • Cause and effect. Words like so, because, therefore, and as a result connect the word to a result. “The ice made the road so treacherous that the school closed.” A road that closes a school must be dangerous.

A contrast clue gives you the opposite of the nearby word. Do not copy the nearby word as the meaning.

check.prompt:
“Although the first apartment Kim saw was spacious, the second one was so small that her couch would not fit through the living room.”

What does spacious mean?
check.hint: What word signals a contrast? The first apartment is the opposite of the second.
check.explain: Although signals a contrast between the two apartments. The second was “so small that her couch would not fit,” so the first must be the opposite: roomy. Replacement test: “Although the first apartment was roomy…” fits. The most tempting wrong answer, “too small for furniture,” copies the clue instead of flipping it.
why: You copied the clue instead of flipping it. Although signals a contrast, so spacious is the opposite of the tiny second apartment.
Nothing in the sentence mentions price. The contrast is about size: a couch that will not fit.
Nothing in the sentence mentions location. The contrast is about size: the second apartment is very small.

screens.title: Words with more than one meaning
screens.html:
Many common words have several meanings: modest, bright, sharp, cold, run, settle, plain. GED questions often say “as used in paragraph 3.” That phrase means: which meaning fits this sentence? The wrong choices are often real meanings of the word that do not fit here.

The replacement test: Cover the word. Put each answer choice in its place. Reread the sentence and the one before it. Keep the choice that makes sense here.

example.prompt: “The pay was modest, but the hours were steady, and Ray liked being home for dinner.” As used here, does modest mean “humble” or “small”?
steps: But sets up a contrast: the pay is a drawback, the hours a benefit.
Test “humble”: “The pay was humble.” Pay cannot be humble about itself. It does not fit.
Test “small”: “The pay was small, but the hours were steady.” It fits.
example.answer: Modest means small or limited here. “Humble” is a real meaning, but it describes people.

check.prompt:
“The doctor was plain with Mr. Ruiz: if he did not stop smoking, his lungs would keep getting worse.”

As used in this sentence, plain most nearly means—
check.hint: Read what comes after the colon. How did the doctor talk to him?
check.explain: The colon introduces exactly what the doctor said, stated bluntly: keep smoking and your lungs get worse. So plain means clear and direct. Replacement test: “The doctor was clear and direct with Mr. Ruiz” fits. The other three are real meanings of plain that do not fit how a person speaks.
why: This is a real meaning (a plain dress), but it describes objects. Put it back: “The doctor was simple and without decoration with Mr. Ruiz” makes no sense.
This is a real meaning (a plain face), but the sentence is about how the doctor spoke, not how she looked.
This is the noun meaning (the Great Plains). Here plain describes the doctor, so it cannot mean a type of land.

screens.title: Denotation and connotation
screens.html:
The denotation of a word is its dictionary meaning. The connotation is the feeling the word carries: positive, negative, or neutral.

PositiveNeutralNegative
thriftycareful with moneycheap
curiousinterestednosy
confidentsure of oneselfarrogant
aromasmellstench

Each row has about the same dictionary meaning, but the feeling is very different. If someone calls you thrifty, it is a compliment. If someone calls you cheap, it is not.

check.prompt: Each word below describes a person who keeps trying and will not give up, or a smell. Drag each word to the feeling it carries.
check.hint: Ask: would I want someone to use this word about me (or about my cooking)?
check.explain: Positive: determined, persistent (praise for not giving up), and fragrance (a pleasant smell). Negative: stubborn and pigheaded (a complaint about someone who will not change). Neutral: smell, which simply names what you notice with your nose. Compare fragrance (pleasant) and stench (awful).
check.why: The most common mistake is putting persistent in Negative because it means about the same as stubborn. Same denotation, different feeling: persistent is praise, stubborn is a complaint.

screens.title: Why did the author choose that word?
screens.html:
When a GED question asks, “Why does the author use the word ___?” or “What does the word ___ suggest?”, it is asking about connotation. Use three steps:

  1. Denotation: what does the word basically mean?
  2. Connotation: is its feeling positive, negative, or neutral? How strong?
  3. Purpose: what does that feeling show about the writer's attitude or the character?

example.prompt: One story calls the mayor's plan “bold.” Another calls the same plan “reckless.” What does each word show?
steps: Denotation: both describe a plan that takes risks.
Connotation: bold is positive (brave); reckless is negative (careless about danger).
Purpose: the first writer approves of the plan; the second writer disapproves.
example.answer: One word can reveal a writer's whole attitude.

check.prompt:
“The new apartment complex towered over the little row of brick houses, blocking their afternoon sun.”

Why does the author most likely use the word towered instead of stood?
check.hint: Picture a tower next to a small house. What feeling does that size difference create?
check.explain: Stood is neutral: it just says where the building is. Towered means rose far above, and it suggests something huge and overpowering. The detail that it blocks the houses' afternoon sun confirms the effect: the little houses are dwarfed. The tempting wrong answer about residents looking down on neighbors goes beyond the text; the word describes the building, not people.
options: to show that the complex was poorly built and might soon fall down
to make the complex seem huge and overpowering beside the houses
to suggest that the brick houses were newer than the complex
to show that the people in the complex looked down on their neighbors
why: Nothing suggests poor building. Towered is about height and power, and blocking the sun supports that.
Towered compares size, not age. Nothing in the sentence says which buildings are newer.
This reads too much into the word. The sentence is about the building's size and shadow, not about how residents treat neighbors.

screens.title: Tone: the writer's attitude
screens.html:
Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude toward the subject. Ask yourself: How does the writer feel about this? Tone words name an attitude:

PositiveNeutralNegative
admiring, affectionate, hopeful, nostalgic, amused, gratefulobjective, matter-of-fact, informativebitter, sarcastic, critical, mocking, resentful, disappointed

Some tones are mixed. A narrator can be affectionate and amused about a messy relative, or bittersweet about something that ended. Sarcasm says the opposite of what the writer means: “Great, another flat tire” is not praise.

check.prompt:
“The new parking garage cost the city $14 million, and it is a marvel of design. Its exits lead straight into a wall, and its elevator stops on only three of its five floors.”

Which word best describes the writer's tone?
check.hint: Do the details match the praise, or do they show the opposite?
check.explain: The writer calls the garage “a marvel of design,” then lists details that show terrible design: exits that lead into a wall and an elevator that skips floors. Saying the opposite of what you mean to criticize something is sarcasm. Students who choose “admiring” take the praise words at face value without checking them against the details.
why: The writer uses praise words (“a marvel of design”), but the details (exits into a wall, a broken elevator plan) show the opposite. That gap is sarcasm, not admiration.
An objective writer reports facts without judging. This writer calls a badly planned garage “a marvel,” which is a clear, mocking judgment.
Nothing looks forward to a better future. The writer is mocking what already exists.

screens.title: Finding tone: highlight, sort, choose
screens.html:
To find the tone of a passage, use three steps:

  1. Highlight the strongest words and details, especially adjectives, verbs, and comparisons.
  2. Sort them. Are they mostly positive, negative, or neutral? Joking or serious?
  3. Choose the most precise word. Avoid extreme answers like furious or ecstatic unless the text is that extreme.

Prove it: you should be able to point to at least two words in the text that support your tone answer.

example.prompt: “Grandma's kitchen always smelled of cinnamon and coffee. I can still see her humming at the stove, flour on her apron, waving me in for one more biscuit.”
steps: Highlight: “always,” “I can still see,” humming, flour on her apron, “one more biscuit.”
Sort: warm, loving details remembered from the past.
Choose: nostalgic and affectionate.
example.answer: Tone: nostalgic and affectionate, proved by “I can still see” and the fond details.

check.prompt:
“I have worked for Mr. Delgado for six years. The warehouse is cold in winter, and the pay is average. When my son was in the hospital, Mr. Delgado covered my shifts himself. I would follow that man anywhere.”

The narrator's tone toward Mr. Delgado is admiring. Which two details best support this? Select two answers.
check.hint: Look for one detail that shows what he did and one that shows how the narrator feels.
check.explain: “Mr. Delgado covered my shifts himself” shows Mr. Delgado going far beyond his job, which is why the narrator admires him. “I would follow that man anywhere” states the admiration directly. The six-year and hospital details are background facts, and “the pay is average” describes the job, not the boss. In fact, it makes the admiration stronger: the narrator stays for Mr. Delgado, not for the money.
options: “I have worked for Mr. Delgado for six years.”
“When my son was in the hospital”
why: This is a plain fact about time. It does not show any feeling about him.
This tells what happened to the son. It sets up the story, but it does not show the narrator's attitude toward Mr. Delgado.
This describes the job, not Mr. Delgado, and it is not positive. It shows that the narrator stays for the boss, not the pay.

screens.title: Mood: the reader's feeling
screens.html:
Mood is the feeling or atmosphere a passage creates in you, the reader. Ask: How does this make me feel? Mood words include tense, eerie, gloomy, peaceful, hopeful, joyful, lonely, cozy.

Writers build mood with setting, light and weather, sounds, the pace of the sentences, and word choice. A paragraph full of short sentences and sudden sounds feels tense. A paragraph of slow, soft details feels calm.

ToneMood
Whose feeling?the writer's or narrator'sthe reader's
AskHow does the writer feel?How do I feel?

A narrator can sound calm (tone) while the reader feels dread (mood).

check.prompt:
“The hallway lights flickered and went out. Somewhere ahead, water dripped in slow, even drops. Kendra counted the doors by touch, one, two, three, and stopped. Behind her, something scraped across the floor.”

Which word best describes the mood of this paragraph?
check.hint: How do you feel when you read the last sentence?
check.explain: The lights go out, water drips in the dark, Kendra feels her way along, and “something scraped across the floor” behind her. These details make the reader feel nervous and eager to know what happens next. The mood is suspenseful. A reader who picks “peaceful” is reacting to one soft detail (the dripping) instead of the whole paragraph.
why: The slow drip could sound calm alone, but darkness and a sudden scrape behind her create fear, not peace.
Nothing in the paragraph is bright or happy. The lights go out and something moves behind her.
Counting doors slowly might seem dull, but it builds suspense: we wait to learn what she will find and what is behind her.

screens.title: Shifts in tone and mood
screens.html:
Moods and tones can change within a passage, and the GED often asks where or how. Watch for these signals:

  • turn words: then, suddenly, but, however, for the first time, at last
  • a new event or a new character arriving
  • a change in light, weather, sound, or setting
  • a new paragraph that starts with a short, sharp sentence

To answer a shift question, name the mood before, find the sentence where it turns, and name the mood after.

example.prompt: “Andre had sat in the same chair for three hours. Every time the doors swung open, his heart leapt. Then a nurse walked toward him, smiling, and for the first time all night, Andre let out his breath.”
steps: Before: tense (three hours of waiting, his heart leaping).
The turn: “Then a nurse walked toward him, smiling…”
After: relief.
example.answer: The mood shifts from tension to relief at the sentence beginning with Then.

check.prompt: Read the paragraph. Click the sentence where the mood shifts from discouraged to hopeful.
check.hint: Find the first sentence that brings good news.
check.explain: Sentences 1 and 2 build discouragement: forty applications, no replies, dread. Sentence 3 is still in that mood: she almost deletes the email. Sentence 4 turns it: a bakery owner offers her a job. Sentence 5 shows the result of the shift (laughing), but the turn itself happens in sentence 4.
spans: Lena had sent out forty applications since March.
Each one disappeared without a reply, and she had started to dread opening her inbox.
On Friday she nearly deleted an email from an unknown address.
It was a bakery owner asking whether she could start on Monday.
Lena read it three times and then called her mother, laughing.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the third sentence. She nearly deletes the email, so the mood is still discouraged; the shift comes when we learn what the email says.

screens.title: Similes and metaphors
screens.html:
Literal language means exactly what it says. Figurative language means more than, or something different from, what it says.

  • A simile compares two unlike things using like or as: “The parking lot was as empty as a ghost town.”
  • A metaphor compares by saying one thing is another, with no like or as: “The parking lot was a desert.”

Not every like or as makes a simile. “I like coffee” and “She sang as she cooked” compare nothing. A simile must compare two different kinds of things.

check.prompt:
“By the end of the double shift, Tomás was a candle burned down to the last half inch.”

Is this a simile or a metaphor? Type simile or metaphor.
check.explain: The sentence says Tomás was a candle, with no like or as, so it is a metaphor. Unpacked: a candle burned almost all the way down has very little left, so Tomás is nearly out of energy.

mistakes.why: Look for like or as: there is none. The sentence says Tomás was a candle, so it is a metaphor.

screens.title: Personification and hyperbole
screens.html:
• Personification gives human actions, feelings, or qualities to something that is not human: “The old floorboards complained under every step.” Floorboards cannot complain, but the word lets you hear the creaking and sense their age.
  • Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humor: “This bag weighs a ton.” “I have told you a million times.” No one means it literally.

To spot personification, find a non-human subject (a machine, the weather, a building, an animal, an idea) and ask whether its verb is something only a person does: sighed, whispered, refused, complained, waited.

check.hint: Which non-human thing does something that people do?
check.explain: In sentence 3, a refrigerator grumbled, which is something an annoyed person does. That is personification: it makes the old refrigerator sound tired and cranky. Sentence 1 is a simile (as hot as). Sentence 2 is hyperbole (enough food for a whole state). Sentence 4 is literal.
spans: The kitchen was as hot as a furnace by noon.
Mom had cooked enough food to feed the entire state.
The ancient refrigerator grumbled every time someone opened its door.
My cousins arrived at two o'clock with three more pies.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the first sentence. It compares the kitchen to a furnace with as, which makes it a simile, not personification.

screens.title: Idioms
screens.html:
An idiom is a common expression whose meaning cannot be figured out from its individual words. “It's raining cats and dogs” means it is raining very hard. “Hit the books” means to study.

If a phrase makes no sense literally, it is probably an idiom. Use the sentences around it to decide what it means.

IdiomMeaning
break the iceease tension at the start of something
on the fenceundecided
spill the beansreveal a secret
jump the gunact too soon
know by hearthave memorized

Idioms are fixed sayings many people use. A metaphor is usually a fresh comparison the writer created.

check.prompt:
Choose the idiom that fits the meaning of the sentence.

“Marcus has not decided whether to take the night class or keep his weekend job. He is still {{0}}.”
check.explain: The first sentence says Marcus “has not decided,” so the idiom must mean undecided. On the fence means exactly that: sitting between two sides without choosing one. The other three are real idioms with different meanings.

why: “Breaking the ice” means easing tension when people first meet. It has nothing to do with being undecided.
“Jumping the gun” means acting too soon. Marcus has not acted at all; he has not decided.
“Spilling the beans” means revealing a secret. Nothing in the sentence involves a secret.

screens.title: Name it, unpack it, explain the effect
screens.html:
GED questions rarely just ask you to name a figure of speech. They ask what it suggests or why the author used it. Use three steps:

  1. Name it. Simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, or idiom?
  2. Unpack it. What two things are compared? List what you know about the second thing.
  3. Explain the effect. Carry those qualities over to the first thing. What does it help you see or feel?

example.prompt: “After my brother left for the Army, hope was a candle my mother kept burning in the front window.”
steps: Name it: metaphor (hope was a candle).
Unpack it: a candle is small but steady, needs tending, and in a window it signals someone to come home.
Effect: her hope is quiet, faithful, and kept alive by effort, waiting for her son's return.
example.answer: The metaphor shows the mother's steady, patient hope.

check.prompt:
“Since the layoffs, the break room has been a library. Nobody jokes, nobody argues about football, and people eat their sandwiches staring at their phones.”

What does the metaphor in the first sentence suggest?
check.hint: What is a library like? Then check the next sentence: why is it that way now?
check.explain: Name it: a metaphor (the break room has been a library). Unpack it: a library is quiet and people do not talk. Effect: the break room is silent and tense. The next sentence confirms it: nobody jokes or argues, and everyone stares at their phones. “Calm and pleasant” is tempting because libraries are peaceful, but the cause, the layoffs, shows the silence is uneasy.
options: The company has turned the break room into a place to read books.
The break room has turned quiet and tense since the layoffs.
Workers are now studying for new jobs during their lunch breaks.
The break room has become a calm and pleasant place to relax.
why: This reads the metaphor literally. Nothing says there are books; the details describe silence.
This adds a reason the passage never gives. The details show silence and phones, not studying.
Quiet is right, but “pleasant” is wrong. Since the layoffs, nobody jokes, which suggests worry, not relaxation.

screens.title: Choosing words that fit the tone
screens.html:
Some GED questions put you in the writer's seat. You read a draft (a letter, a notice, a newsletter article) and choose the word or phrase that fits both the meaning and the tone. All the choices may mean about the same thing. The difference is the feeling.

  1. Name the purpose and audience: a tribute? a complaint? a formal notice?
  2. Sort each choice: positive, negative, or neutral? formal or casual?
  3. Pick the one that matches the purpose. Cut slang in formal writing and negative words in praise.

check.prompt:
A clinic is writing a formal letter thanking a donor. Choose the best word or phrase for each blank.

“Your {{0}} gift of $5,000 will allow us to keep our doors open on Saturdays. Our patients are {{1}} for your support.”
check.hint: Ask: is this word positive, and is it formal enough for a thank-you letter to a donor?
check.explain: The purpose is formal thanks. Generous praises the donor's kindness; the other choices describe a large amount but suggest spending too much or sound casual. Deeply grateful is strong and formal; the others are slang or weaken the thanks with pretty or kind of.

why: Extravagant suggests spending too much, which sounds like criticism of the donor.
Hefty is casual and focuses on size, as if commenting on a big bill. It is not warm enough for a thank-you.
Excessive means more than is reasonable, which is a clear criticism. It insults the donor.
“Super stoked” is slang. It is too casual for a formal letter.
“Pretty” weakens the thanks and sounds casual.
“Kind of” makes the thanks sound unsure, which is the wrong tone for a donor.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • Find a word's meaning in context with definition, example, contrast, and cause-and-effect clues. A contrast clue gives the opposite.
  • On “as used in” questions, use the replacement test. Watch for real meanings of the word that do not fit this sentence.
  • Denotation is the dictionary meaning. Connotation is the positive, negative, or neutral feeling. “Why did the author use ___?” is a connotation question.
  • Tone is the writer's attitude. Mood is the reader's feeling. Highlight, sort, choose a precise word, and prove it with two words from the text. Avoid extremes.
  • For a shift, name the mood before, find the turn, name the mood after.
  • Simile (like/as), metaphor (is), personification (human action), hyperbole (exaggeration), idiom (fixed saying). Name it, unpack it, explain the effect.
  • In drafts, choose the word whose meaning and tone fit the purpose.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Last Call at the Blue Kettle
stimuli.html:
[1] The bell over the door of the Blue Kettle had rung for thirty-one years, and tonight Marisol Ortega wanted to hear it one more time. She stood behind the counter with a rag in her hand, wiping a spot that was already clean. Outside, the rain came down in gray sheets, and the parking lot was as empty as a church on a Monday.

[2] The diner had been her husband's dream before it was hers. Ernesto had bought it with a bank loan, a borrowed truck, and more nerve than sense. “You two will be eating beans until you're fifty,” her sister had warned. Ernesto only laughed. He painted the walls the color of butter and hung a sign in the window that promised COFFEE HOT AS GOSSIP. For years the place hummed. Truckers, nurses coming off the night shift, teenagers splitting a single plate of fries four ways: they all found their way to the Blue Kettle. The long counter was the town's front porch, and Ernesto knew every one of their orders by heart.

[3] Now a highway bypass had opened two miles east, and the traffic had dried up like a creek in August. Ernesto had been gone for three years. The landlord had been polite but firm. Marisol had signed the papers on Tuesday. Tomorrow a crew would come for the grill.

[4] She turned off the neon sign in the window. Without its pink glow, the room looked smaller and older. The stools stood in a crooked line like old men waiting for a bus that would never come. The coffee maker sighed as it cooled. Somewhere in the back, the ice machine dropped one last batch of cubes with a sound like scattered applause.

[5] Marisol thought about the night of the big ice storm, when the power went out across the county and half the town crowded into the diner because Ernesto had a gas stove and a stubborn streak. He had cooked by candlelight until dawn. People still stopped her at the grocery store to talk about that night. “Your husband kept us all afloat,” one woman told her once, squeezing her hand. Marisol had not trusted her voice to answer.

[6] The bell rang.

[7] She looked up, ready to say they were closed. In the doorway stood Danny Pruitt, rain dripping from the brim of his cap. He had been one of those teenagers splitting fries. Now he had gray in his beard and a boy of about ten beside him.

[8] “Heard tonight was the last night,” Danny said. “I wanted him to see it. Before.”

[9] Marisol looked at the boy, who was staring at the pie case as if it held treasure. Then she looked at the cold grill, the stacked chairs, the mop bucket by the door. She had planned to be finished by now. She had planned to go home, sit in the quiet, and let it be over.

[10] She reached up and switched the neon sign back on.

[11] “Sit anywhere,” she said. “The coffee's still hot.”
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: The Deep End
stimuli.html:
[1] I learned to swim the year I turned thirty-eight, which is a little like learning to ride a bike the year you get your driver's license. For most of my life, I had treated water the way some people treat dogs that bark behind fences: I kept my distance and pretended I was not afraid.

[2] My excuse had always been practical. I grew up in a town where the only pool belonged to a motel, and the motel did not welcome kids from my street. By the time I was an adult, not swimming had hardened into part of who I was, like a crooked tooth I had stopped noticing. Then my daughter, Keisha, joined a swim team, and I found myself sitting in the bleachers every Saturday, cheering for something I could not do.

[3] The adult beginner class met at 6 a.m. at the community pool on Fulton Street. There were five of us: a retired mail carrier, two college students, a man who drove a forklift, and me. Our instructor, Ms. Abernathy, was about five feet tall and had a voice that could cut through a thunderstorm. On the first morning, she told us to put our faces in the water and blow bubbles. I felt ridiculous. I also could not do it. Every time my nose touched the surface, my whole body staged a protest.

[4] “Your body is not your enemy,” Ms. Abernathy said. “It's just a nervous employee. Give it clear instructions.”

[5] So I gave it instructions. Breathe in. Face down. Breathe out slowly. Week by week, the water stopped feeling like a wall and started feeling like a place. By the fifth week, I could float on my back, staring up at the water-stained ceiling tiles, my ears full of the pool's low hum. By the eighth, I could swim one awkward, splashing length of the pool. It was not pretty. The forklift driver said I swam like a shopping cart with a bad wheel, and he was not wrong.

[6] The last class ended with a test: swim across the deep end, where the floor drops to twelve feet. I stood at the edge with my toes curled over the tile. My heart was pounding so hard I was sure the others could hear it. Then I looked at Keisha, who had insisted on coming that morning and was sitting in the bleachers, and I jumped.

[7] I would love to report that I glided across like a dolphin. I did not. I thrashed, I swallowed half the pool, and I reached the far wall in what Ms. Abernathy generously called “a time.” But I reached it. When I looked up, my daughter was on her feet, shouting my name as if I had just won a gold medal.

[8] I still swim on Saturdays. I am still slow. But the water and I have reached an understanding, and that is more than I ever expected.
stimuli.source: Original personal narrative written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Draft Article: Volunteer Spotlight
stimuli.html:
Volunteer Spotlight: Gloria Haines
(Draft article for the Grace Street Community Center newsletter)

(1) This month's Volunteer Spotlight shines on Gloria Haines, who has run the Saturday food pantry at the Grace Street Community Center for six years. (2) Every week, Gloria arrives at 7 a.m. to unload the delivery truck, sort donations, and set up tables before the doors open. (3) Families who visit the pantry say Gloria is (A); she remembers their children's names and always asks how they are doing.

(4) Gloria's dedication is clearest in a crisis. (5) When the pantry's only freezer broke down last July, Gloria (B) and raised $1,200 from neighbors and local businesses in a single weekend. (6) Not one pound of donated food was lost. (7) Gloria is just as careful with the pantry's money: she is famously (D), comparing prices at three wholesalers before every order so that each donated dollar buys as much food as possible.

(8) New volunteers say Gloria (E) during their first weeks, showing them where everything is stored and introducing them to the regular families. (9) Ask anyone at the center, and they will tell you the same thing: Gloria is (C). (10) Volunteers who would like to work alongside her can sign up at the front desk.

stimuli.title: First Shift
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] At 5:52 a.m., Renata Cruz stood outside the gate of the Halvorsen Foods plant with a lunch bag in one hand and her new badge in the other. She was forty-one years old, and she had not punched a time clock since before her twins were born. The badge photo made her look startled, which, she thought, was at least honest.

[2] Inside, the plant floor was an ocean of noise. Conveyor belts rattled, compressors hissed, and a buzzer went off every few seconds for no reason anyone explained. Bags of frozen vegetables slid past at the speed of a fast walk. Renata's stomach dropped. She had told her husband she could handle anything after raising twins. Now she wondered whether she was in over her head.

[3] Her trainer was a small, gray-haired woman named Mrs. Okoye, who had more patience than words. She showed Renata how to check the seals, how to pull a bad bag without stopping the line, and how to stack the cases so they would not tip. When Renata fumbled a bag and three more piled up behind it, Mrs. Okoye simply reached over, cleared them, and nodded at her to try again.

[4] By ten o'clock, Renata's feet ached and her fingers were numb from the cold product. The line kept coming, bag after bag, as steady as rain. Across the floor, the forklift drivers moved through the aisles like dancers who had rehearsed for years. The big freezer door groaned open and shut behind them. Renata kept her eyes on the seals.

[5] At lunch she sat alone at the end of a long table and ate half a sandwich without tasting it. She thought about the twins' first day of kindergarten, when Miguel had clung to the classroom door. She had told him that everyone is new once. She had not expected to need the advice herself.

[6] In the last hour, something changed. Renata stopped thinking about each motion. Her hands found the bad seals before her eyes did. When a split bag came down the line, she pulled it and caught the next one without looking up. Mrs. Okoye, passing behind her, paused and said only, “Good.”

[7] At 2:30 the buzzer sounded for shift change. Someone held the door for her. A man from the forklift crew asked if she was coming back tomorrow, and she heard herself laugh and say, “Try and stop me.”

[8] Outside, the sun was finally up. Renata found her badge in her pocket and looked at the photo again. She still looked startled in it. She did not feel startled anymore.

stimuli.title: Middle C
stimuli.source: Original personal narrative written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] My granddaughter, Imani, started piano lessons at seven, and by nine she could play songs I recognized. I was fifty-three, and I could play the doorbell. So when the community college offered a class called Piano for the Absolute Beginner, I signed up before I could talk myself out of it.

[2] The class met on Tuesday nights in a room with twelve electronic keyboards and one real piano that nobody was allowed to touch. Our teacher, Mr. Feld, was a retired band director with enormous eyebrows and endless patience. On the first night, he asked us to place our right thumb on middle C. I placed mine on the wrong C, which, I learned, is a surprisingly easy thing to do when there are eight of them.

[3] My hands, it turned out, did not want to cooperate with each other. My left hand would hold a note perfectly well until my right hand tried to do anything at all, and then the left hand would quit in sympathy. Mr. Feld called this “a common challenge.” My wife, listening from the kitchen at home, called it something else.

[4] Still, I practiced: twenty minutes every morning before work, with headphones on so my wife could drink her coffee in peace. The scales were dull, and my fingers felt as if they belonged to a stranger. But week by week, the stranger got friendlier. By October I could play “Ode to Joy” with both hands, slowly, as long as nobody watched and nobody breathed.

[5] At the end of the term, Mr. Feld held a recital for families. I would play a two-minute piece, the longest thing I had ever attempted. When my turn came, I sat down at the real piano, the one we were never allowed to touch, and my mind went perfectly blank. I missed the first chord. I missed the third one, too. Somewhere in the second line, I found my place and held on to it the way a man holds a railing on an icy staircase.

[6] When I finished, there was a short silence. Then Imani stood up in the second row and clapped as if I had just played Carnegie Hall.

[7] I am still a beginner. I still find the wrong C now and then. But the keyboard and I are on speaking terms now, and some mornings it even seems glad to see me.

stimuli.title: Draft Article: Thank You, Nurse Pauline
stimuli.html:
Thank You, Nurse Pauline
(Draft article for the Eastside Health Clinic staff newsletter)

(1) After twenty-seven years at Eastside Health Clinic, Pauline Mercer, RN, will retire at the end of this month. (2) Pauline has worked the clinic's walk-in hours longer than anyone, checking in patients, taking vital signs, and answering the questions patients were too nervous to ask the doctor. (3) Patients describe her as (A); she listens to every worry, no matter how small, and never makes anyone feel rushed.

(4) Pauline is also (D) about patient privacy. (5) She never discusses a case outside the exam room, and she taught a generation of staff to do the same.

(6) Pauline was at her best on the day the clinic's computer system crashed during last October's flu clinic. (7) With forty patients in the waiting room, she (B), pulled out paper charts, and set up a sign-in line that kept everyone moving. (8) Every patient received a flu shot that day.

(9) Many of our newer nurses say Pauline (E) when they arrived, answering their questions and checking on them after hard shifts. (10) Ask anyone here, and they will tell you that Pauline is (C). (11) Please join us for a farewell lunch in the staff room on Friday, May 30, at noon.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the narrator says that Ernesto “knew every one of their orders by heart.” What does this phrase mean?
items.hint: “By heart” is an idiom. It has nothing to do with the heart as an organ or with feelings.
items.explain:
Step 1. Recognize the idiom. Read literally, “knew by heart” does not make sense, so it is a common expression with its own meaning.

Step 2. “To know something by heart” means to have it memorized. Check the context: the same customers (truckers, nurses, teenagers) came again and again, so Ernesto would have learned their usual orders.

Step 3. Replacement test: “Ernesto had memorized every one of their orders.” It fits.

The main trap: “cared deeply about his customers and their feelings” reads the word heart literally. He may have cared about them, but that is not what this phrase means.
options: He had memorized what each regular customer usually ordered.
He cared deeply about his regular customers and their feelings.
He wrote down each order carefully before he started cooking it.
He served his customers only the dishes that he loved the most.
why: This reads heart literally, as if the phrase were about feelings. “By heart” is an idiom that means “from memory.”
Writing orders down is the opposite of knowing them by heart. Nothing in the passage mentions writing anything down.
Nothing in the passage says what Ernesto liked to cook. This choice also misreads heart as being about what he loved.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the author writes that the parking lot was “as empty as a church on a Monday.” This phrase is an example of—
items.hint: Look for the signal word that comes before “a church.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the two things being compared: the parking lot and a church on a Monday (when most churches are empty).

Step 2. Look for the signal word. The comparison uses as (“as empty as”). A comparison of two unlike things using like or as is a simile.

Step 3. Rule out the others. A metaphor would say the lot was a church. Personification would give the lot a human action. An idiom is a fixed common saying; this comparison is the author's own.
why: A metaphor says one thing is another, with no like or as. This phrase uses “as … as,” so it is a simile.
Personification gives a human action to something non-human. The parking lot does nothing human here; it is only compared to a church.
An idiom is a fixed saying many people use. This is a fresh comparison the author created, built with as, so it is a simile.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 4 that uses personification: it describes an object doing something only a person can do, without making a comparison using like or as.
items.hint: Which object is described with an action people do when they are tired or sad?
items.explain:
Step 1. Personification gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human.

Step 2. In “The coffee maker sighed as it cooled,” a machine sighs, which is something a tired or sad person does. There is no comparison with like or as; here as means “while.”

Step 3. Rule out the others. Sentences 1 and 2 are literal. The stools and ice-machine sentences use like to compare, so they are similes.

Effect: the sighing coffee maker makes even the machines seem tired and sad, adding to the feeling that the diner is ending.
spans: She turned off the neon sign in the window.
Without its pink glow, the room looked smaller and older.
The stools stood in a crooked line like old men waiting for a bus that would never come.
The coffee maker sighed as it cooled.
Somewhere in the back, the ice machine dropped one last batch of cubes with a sound like scattered applause.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the stools sentence. It compares the stools to old men, but it uses like, so it is a simile. In the coffee maker sentence, as means “while,” not a comparison.

items.prompt:
The article is meant to honor Gloria. Choose the word that best completes blank (D) in sentence 7.

Gloria is just as careful with the pantry's money: she is famously {{0}}, comparing prices at three wholesalers before every order so that each donated dollar buys as much food as possible.
items.hint: All four words mean “spends little.” Which one is a compliment?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the clue after the colon: she compares prices so that every donated dollar buys as much food as possible. That is careful, wise spending.

Step 2. All four words share a denotation: someone who spends little. They differ in connotation. Cheap, stingy, and tightfisted are negative.

Step 3. The article honors Gloria, so the positive word fits: thrifty, which means careful with money in a good way.

why: Cheap has the same basic meaning (spends little), but it suggests she is unwilling to spend, which is an insult. It does not fit an article that honors her.
Stingy means unwilling to give or share. It is negative, and it contradicts the point: she saves money so the pantry can give more food.
Tightfisted means unwilling to part with money. It is negative and does not fit a tribute.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the narrator says Ernesto bought the diner with “more nerve than sense.” What does this phrase suggest about Ernesto?
items.hint: Here, nerve means courage, and sense means good judgment. Also look at how his sister reacts.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the meaning of each key word in context. Nerve means courage or daring (“it took nerve to do that”). Sense means careful, practical judgment.

Step 2. Put it together: he had more courage than caution. The context supports this: he used a loan and a borrowed truck, his sister warned they would be “eating beans until you're fifty,” and he “only laughed.”

Step 3. The phrase has a fond, slightly teasing connotation: the risk was not sensible, but it was brave.

The main trap is “nervous,” which mixes up nerve with nervous.
options: He was brave enough to take a big risk that was not very wise.
He was a nervous man who was easily upset when problems came up at work.
He knew very little about cooking or running a restaurant when he bought it.
He was dishonest with the bank about how much money he had saved up.
why: This confuses nerve (courage, daring) with nervous (anxious). Ernesto “only laughed” at his sister's warning, which is not how a nervous man acts.
Sense here means good judgment about risk, not cooking skill. The passage never says he lacked restaurant experience.
Nothing in the passage suggests lying. He used a bank loan and a borrowed truck; the risk was in the plan, not in dishonesty.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the author writes that “the traffic had dried up like a creek in August.” What does this comparison suggest?
items.hint: Picture what happens to a small stream during the hottest, driest month. Then apply that to traffic.
items.explain:
Step 1. Name it: a simile (it uses like). Traffic is compared to a creek in August.

Step 2. Unpack it: in the heat of late summer, a creek slowly loses water until little or none is left. The shared quality is a flow that shrinks and disappears.

Step 3. Apply it to the context: a bypass opened two miles east, so the cars that once flowed past the diner now go elsewhere.

The wrong choices all take the comparison literally (real water, real summer, real heat).
options: The cars passing the diner had slowly dwindled to almost none.
The road in front of the diner flooded with water every summer.
The diner lost most of its customers only during the summer months.
Drivers stayed away because the weather near the diner was too hot.
why: This takes the creek literally, and it even reverses it: a creek in August dries up; it does not flood. The simile describes traffic, not water.
This takes “August” literally. The simile describes how the traffic shrank, and paragraph 3 says the cause was the new bypass, not the season.
This reads the comparison as a weather report. Paragraph 3 blames the highway bypass that opened two miles east, not the heat.

items.prompt: Drag each phrase from the story into the category that names the type of figurative language it uses.
items.hint: Check for like or as making a comparison first. Then ask: does it say one thing is another? Does an object act like a person? Is it a common saying?
items.explain:
“as empty as a church on a Monday” → Simile: compares the parking lot to a church using as.

“The long counter was the town's front porch” → Metaphor: says the counter was a front porch, a friendly place where neighbors sat and talked.

“The coffee maker sighed as it cooled” → Personification: a machine is given a human action.

“knew every one of their orders by heart” → Idiom: a common expression meaning “from memory.”

“with a sound like scattered applause” → Simile: compares the sound of falling ice to clapping using like.
choices: “as empty as a church on a Monday”
“The long counter was the town's front porch”
“The coffee maker sighed as it cooled”
“knew every one of their orders by heart”
items.why: The most common wrong placement is putting the coffee maker in Simile because of the word as. Here as means “while”; the figure of speech is the machine sighing.

items.prompt: Which phrase best describes the mood the author creates in paragraph 4?
items.hint: Highlight the descriptive details in paragraph 4. Are they mostly about energy, danger, or emptiness?
items.explain:
Step 1. Highlight the strongest details: without the glow the room looks “smaller and older”; the stools are “like old men waiting for a bus that would never come”; the coffee maker “sighed”; the ice machine drops “one last batch.”

Step 2. Sort them. These details describe emptiness, age, hopeless waiting, and endings. They make the reader feel sad and alone with Marisol.

Step 3. The precise words: lonely and sorrowful. “Tense and frightening” is the most tempting wrong answer because of the night and rain, but nothing in the paragraph is a threat.
